31:1.text: Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.

provenance.other: 'Dumb idols' occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Habakkuk 2:18, where they are what the maker of a graven image makes, and 1 Corinthians 12:2. Only the Corinthians verse joins them to a verb of leading.
provenance.alternative: Habakkuk 2:18-19 supplies the phrase and a 'teacher of lies' who is a plausible model for Zoram; but it has no leading, and the whole of its verbal contact is the two words.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about people who are being reminded what they used to be — Gentiles, carried away, led. Alma 31:1 puts the Zoramites in exactly that grammatical position: they are not idolaters who chose, they are people being led, and the man doing the leading is named in the same clause. The chapter that follows shows the mechanism, which is a liturgy performed once a week and never mentioned again (31:23); Paul's 'even as ye were led' is the KJV's one comment on how that happens.

31:1.note: 'Zoram, which was their leader, was leading the hearts of the people to bow down to dumb idols.' Two words of a KJV pair plus the verb that governs them in one of the two. The Zoramite apostasy as the chapter describes it is not in fact idolatrous — there is no image on the Rameumptom, only a creed — so the phrase is doing work the narrative does not support, which is itself the reason to think it is borrowed rather than observed. Well below any quotation threshold; the case is the collocation of 'dumb idols' with 'led'.

31:5.text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

provenance.other: Hebrews 4:12 is the one KJV verse that measures the word of God against a sword. “than any twoedged sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Alma 12:7 already took the last clause of this verse — 'the thoughts and intents of the heart' — as a six-word singleton. Here the same verse is used at its other end, and the argument the book makes from it is the argument Hebrews makes: the word is more powerful than the sword. Alma has just prosecuted a war, and the sentence that sends him to Antionum with five men instead of an army is a paraphrase of the verse in which scripture says why that is the better weapon.

31:5.note: 'It had had more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword … therefore Alma thought it was expedient that they should try the virtue of the word of God.' No run of shared words, but three of Hebrews 4:12's terms in its own relation: the word of God, powerful, and the sword it outmatches. This is a second use of a verse already adjudicated in this book at 12:7, and it is written as a link rather than a cross-reference because it draws on a different clause and makes a different argument — 12:7 borrowed the discerner of thoughts, 31:5 borrows the comparison with the sword. 'Try the virtue of' is not KJV; the KJV's 'virtue' is the power that goes out of Jesus (Mark 5:30), and the sense here is the modern one of testing an efficacy.
31:5.whyNot: The verbal contact is a paraphrase, not a run, and the proposition that preaching works better than fighting needs no source. A reader who takes 12:7 as this book's only use of Hebrews 4:12 would decline this row.

31:10.text: Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

provenance.other: 'Enter into temptation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 26:41 and Luke 22:40, both Gethsemane. 'Prayer and supplication' occurs in five, of which Acts 1:14 alone has it as a continuing corporate practice — 'these all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication'.
provenance.significance: The Zoramites' fault is stated as the neglect of two New Testament habits fused into one sentence: the church's continuance in prayer at Acts 1:14, and the reason for praying that Jesus gives in Gethsemane. Recover the Gethsemane context and the failure described is the disciples' own — they were told to pray that they enter not into temptation and they slept. Alma 31:10 makes the Zoramite congregation the sleeping disciples, which is a milder charge than idolatry and a more accurate description of what the chapter goes on to show: a people who pray once a week and then never speak of God again (31:23).

31:10.note: 'Neither would they observe the performances of the church, to continue in prayer and supplication to God daily, that they might not enter into temptation.' Two New Testament phrases in one clause. 'Continue in prayer and supplication' is Acts 1:14's description of the first church at prayer, and 'enter into temptation' belongs to two KJV verses, both of which are Jesus in Gethsemane telling his disciples why to pray. The Book of Mormon has 'that they might not enter' where Matthew has 'that ye enter not', a person-shift the new setting requires; Luke 22:40's shorter form ('Pray that ye enter not into temptation') is equally close and the two cannot be separated on this wording.

31:13.text: For Solomon had made a brasen scaffold of five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high, and had set it in the midst of the court: and upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands toward heaven.

provenance.other: 'Scaffold' and 'in the midst of the court' are each KJV singletons, and both are in this verse. The KJV's only other purpose-built platform for public religious speech is Ezra's 'pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose' (Nehemiah 8:4, also a singleton), which is for reading the law rather than for prayer. “scaffold” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “in the midst of the court” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are 2 Chronicles 6:13.
provenance.significance: There is exactly one raised structure in the KJV built so that one man may stand on it, in the middle of a sanctuary court, and pray with his hands spread toward heaven, and it is Solomon's at the dedication of the temple. The Rameumptom is that structure with one thing changed. Solomon 'stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel'; the Zoramite stands and does not kneel, on a top that 'would only admit one person', which removes the congregation the scaffold was built to face. Read that way the chapter's satire is precise rather than general: the Zoramites have not invented a heathen altar, they have reproduced the furniture of the temple dedication and deleted from it the two gestures — kneeling, and standing before the people — that made Solomon's prayer intercession rather than display.

31:13.note: 'They had a place built up in the centre of their synagogue, a place of standing, which was high above the head; and the top thereof would only admit one person.' No run of shared words, and the strength of the row is entirely in the rarity of what is being described. Two KJV singletons, 'scaffold' and 'in the midst of the court', sit in the one verse that describes a raised standing-place set in the middle of a sanctuary, and the next verse of Alma supplies its posture: stand upon the top, stretch forth the hands toward heaven. The Book of Mormon's 'centre' for the KJV's 'midst' is the sort of substitution that hides a borrowing from an n-gram search, and this candidate appeared in no machine stream.

31:14.text: And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the LORD. And, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake:

provenance.other: 'Go forth and stand upon' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Spread forth his hands toward heaven' is Solomon's gesture at 1 Kings 8:22 and 2 Chronicles 6:13; the Book of Mormon reads 'stretch forth', which is the KJV's verb for Moses' hand toward heaven in the plagues (Exodus 9:22, 10:21) rather than for prayer.
provenance.significance: The instruction to go forth and stand is given once in the KJV, to Elijah at Horeb, and what it introduces is the discovery that God is not in the wind, not in the earthquake and not in the fire, but in a still small voice. The Zoramite obeys the same instruction and then cries with a loud voice. Nothing in the chapter says this; the two verses put side by side say it. The Rameumptom liturgy is the exact inversion of the one KJV scene in which a man is told to stand on a height and wait for God, and the inversion is in the volume.

31:14.note: 'Whosoever desired to worship, must go forth and stand upon the top thereof, and stretch forth his hands towards heaven, and cry with a loud voice.' The five-word run 'go forth and stand upon' is a KJV singleton, and Alma keeps its syntax exactly, swapping Horeb's mount for the top of the stand. The candidate was in the machine stream (rarity 3.00, the highest score in the chapter) and the stream had no way to see why it mattered. The gesture in the second half of the verse is Solomon's from 2 Chronicles 6:13, which is the verse behind 31:13; so the sentence is built out of the KJV's two great scenes of a man standing raised up before God, one of them a temple dedication and one of them a theophany, with the loud voice supplied by neither.
31:14.whyNot: 'Go forth' and 'stand upon' are both common, and their collocation could be independent. If 31:13's link to 2 Chronicles 6:13 is declined, this row loses most of its context score with it.

31:15.text: And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.

provenance.other: The doubled 'holy, holy' occurs in two KJV verses, Isaiah 6:3 and Revelation 4:8, and in both it is trebled.
provenance.significance: If the Rameumptom prayer opens with the seraphic acclamation docked by one, the docking is the point: a liturgy that has lost a third of its Trisagion, addressed by men on a platform to a God they immediately deny has a Son. Isaiah 6 is also the chapter in which the prophet is sent to a people whose heart is made fat and whose ears are heavy, which is the diagnosis Alma reaches by 31:24-27 in his own words.

31:15.note: 'Holy, holy God; we believe that thou art God, and we believe that thou art holy.' The doubled vocative is the KJV's only formula of its kind, and it is the opening of the one prayer in this chapter we are given verbatim. Recorded at echo, not allusion: two words, a truncation of the source, and a form of address common in English devotion independently of the KJV. Worth the row because of where it sits — the first line of the liturgy the whole chapter exists to describe — and not because of its length.
31:15.whyNot: 'Holy' repeated in direct address to God is not distinctive enough to identify a source, and the truncation to two removes precisely what makes Isaiah 6:3 and Revelation 4:8 recognisable.

31:17.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

provenance.route: Hebrews 13:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon; 'but thou art the same' from Psalm 102:27 / Hebrews 1:12
provenance.other: 'The same yesterday' and 'and to day and for ever' are each KJV singletons, both in Hebrews 13:8. 'But thou art the same' occurs in exactly two verses, Psalm 102:27 and its quotation at Hebrews 1:12. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between those two at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces; the epistle is preferred because the clause it is welded to is Hebrews' own.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's finding. The sentence immediately before it is 'thou hast made it known unto us that there shall be no Christ' — and the sentence that follows the denial is the KJV's single most compact assertion that Christ does not change. Two Hebrews verses are fused: the opening address of Psalm 102:27, which Hebrews 1:12 applies to the Son, and the whole of Hebrews 13:8, which names him. Strip 'Jesus Christ' from Hebrews 13:8 and the remainder becomes a creed about an immutable spirit; that subtraction is exactly what the Zoramites have performed, and the words they are left with are still his. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the suppressed correspondence here is a proper name.

31:17.note: 'And thou hast made it known unto us that there shall be no Christ; but thou art the same, yesterday, to-day, and forever.' Seven words of Hebrews 13:8 in order, minus the subject, prefixed by the clause the KJV uses to introduce the same idea at Psalm 102:27 and Hebrews 1:12. Two KJV singletons stand in the borrowed run. The 1830 hyphenation 'to-day' preserves the KJV's two-word 'to day' more visibly than the modern text's 'today'. This is well under Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six long quotations; it is catalogued as a quotation because a complete KJV predicate is reproduced with only its subject removed, and because the removal is the argument.

31:18.text: The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.

provenance.other: 'God, I thank thee' is a KJV singleton. 'A chosen generation … an holy nation' is 1 Peter 2:9, itself a singleton for 'a chosen generation'; 'an holy people' and its cognates are too widely spread in Deuteronomy to identify a source. “God I thank thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “a chosen generation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The Rameumptom prayer is Luke 18:11 with its two variables filled in. The Pharisee 'stood and prayed thus with himself' — and the Zoramite structure is named, in the text's own gloss, 'the Holy Stand', a place of standing whose top admits one person and which therefore makes praying with oneself architectural. The parable's thanksgiving turns on a comparison with a named other; the Zoramite's turns on 'while others shall perish' (31:28). What the borrowing adds to Luke is the missing publican: Alma's answer at 33:11 will be a man who cries for mercy from outside the synagogue, and Luke 18:13's publican 'standing afar off' is the shape of that answer before it is given.

31:18.note: 'We thank thee, O God, that we are a chosen and a holy people. Amen.' The four-word run 'God, I thank thee' is a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon has it in the plural with the vocative moved: 'We thank thee, O God, that…'. The clause it governs is 1 Peter 2:9's description of the church, so the prayer is Luke's Pharisee praying in Peter's vocabulary. Alma 4:12 already used this parable, from its frame at 18:9 ('trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others'); this row is written in full rather than cross-referenced because it is the parable's actual prayer rather than Luke's summary of it, and because the second use is the argument — 4:12 diagnosed the Nephite church, and 31:18 gives an entire people the Pharisee's words to say aloud once a week. Alma quotes the line back at 31:28 with 'while others shall perish' added, which is the parable's comparison restored.

31:27.text: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:13, or its quotation at Matthew 15:8, or its transcription at 2 Nephi 27:25 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The verse exists three ways in this project's corpus: Isaiah 29:13, Matthew 15:8 / Mark 7:6, and 2 Nephi 27:25, where the Book of Mormon transcribes the Isaiah form. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence — Alma 31:27 reproduces nothing at a point where the versions differ — so the mediation cannot be settled from this verse.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:13's complaint has two halves, mouth and heart, and Alma 31:27 sets them against each other in the same order: 'they cry unto thee with their mouths, while … their hearts are swallowed up in their pride.' The half of Isaiah that Alma does not use is the third clause, 'their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men' — which is what the Zoramite liturgy demonstrably is, a prayer every man recites word for word (31:20, 31:22). The unquoted clause is the one that fits the chapter best.

31:27.note: 'They cry unto thee with their mouths, while they are puffed up.' The mouth-against-heart antithesis is Isaiah 29:13's and the sequence is his, but no run survives: Alma has 'cry' for 'draw near', a plural 'mouths' for the KJV's singular, and 'puffed up' from Paul in place of the removed heart. Recorded as an echo at moderate for that reason. The chapter's other half of the figure is at 31:17, where the Zoramites say a belief in Christ 'doth lead their hearts to wander far from thee' — Isaiah's 'removed their heart far from me' with the charge turned around, which is worth more to the case than anything in 31:27 itself.
31:27.whyNot: Every word Alma shares with Isaiah 29:13 is common, and the mediation check returned no decisive point. A reader could take the antithesis as an independent commonplace of prophetic rebuke.

31:37.text: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

provenance.other: 'Take no thought' occurs in five KJV verses and 'what ye shall eat' in three; the three-membered eat/drink/put on series occurs only at Matthew 6:25. mediation-check.py is decisive for Matthew over Luke 12:22: the Book of Mormon has 'or what ye shall drink', which Luke's version of the saying does not contain. “what ye shall put on” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:25 and Luke 12:22.
provenance.significance: The Sermon on the Mount's next verse is the reason the command can be obeyed — 'Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not … yet your heavenly Father feedeth them' — and Alma 31:38 supplies exactly that: 'And the Lord provided for them.' So the Book of Mormon has taken two consecutive verses of Matthew 6 and turned them into a narrative sequence, command then fulfilment, which is what a sermon cannot do and a history can. The care taken over the third member of the series is what makes the row certain rather than probable: Luke tells the same saying without the drink, and this is Matthew's.

31:37.note: 'Taking no thought for themselves what they should eat, or what they should drink, or what they should put on.' Fourteen words of Matthew 6:25 in order with only the pronoun and tense changed — 'they should' for 'ye shall' throughout — and with Matthew's three-part series intact. The series is the evidence: the same saying at Luke 12:22 has two members, eat and put on, and the mediation check finds the Book of Mormon on Matthew's side at the one point where the two Gospels differ. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

31:38.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun smite them: for he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall he guide them.

provenance.other: 'Shall not hunger' and 'hunger nor thirst' are each KJV singletons, both at Isaiah 49:10; 'hunger no more' is a singleton at Revelation 7:16, which quotes it. mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for the Old Testament form: Alma lacks Revelation's 'any more'. Against that, the 'neither' joining the two verbs is Revelation's and not Isaiah's, so the row is written as direct-OT with the counter-evidence named rather than suppressed. “hunger nor thirst” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “hunger no more” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 7:16 supplies the conjunction and is elsewhere a live source in this book (Alma 5:21, 13:11 both use Revelation 7:14); the promise there is made to those who came out of great tribulation, which fits missionaries sent into affliction as well as Isaiah's returning exiles do.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 49 is the chapter the Book of Mormon transcribed whole at 1 Nephi 21, so its wording is available to this book at first hand and not only through the KJV. What Isaiah 49:10 promises is safe passage to people being brought home from exile; Alma 31 applies it to five men and two sons walking into a land that has separated itself from them. The promise of the return is spent on the mission that goes the other way.

31:38.note: 'And the Lord provided for them that they should hunger not, neither should they thirst.' Two KJV singletons, 'shall not hunger' and 'hunger nor thirst', both belong to Isaiah 49:10, and the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's negation rather than Revelation 7:16's 'no more … any more' — which is the one point at which the mediation check can decide, and it decides for Isaiah. The verse also completes the borrowing begun at 31:37: Matthew's command not to take thought for food and drink, then Isaiah's promise that they shall have both.
